Just six games into his first-grade career, rookie halfback Zane Harrison announced himself as one to watch in the NRL, stepping up to slot the winning field as the Titans upset the Panthers. Still only 20, Harrison showed remarkable composure to seal the 19-18 win with 13 seconds remaining, showing no sign of nerves as he settle himself to land the decisive blow. Just a few moments earlier however, he had tried to do the same thing, only to miscue the kick poorly, barely getting the ball off the ground. “My first one was a proper shank, so I knew I had to nail the second one,” Harrison said. As it happened: Critta snatches victory for Dogs; Titans win thriller; Dolphins in 7 heaven “I still had confidence that I've done the work and that I'd nail that one. “It was a good result and it's good to come off like that.” Overall, it was a breakout performance from the former schoolboys star who started this season playing for his junior club Tweed Seagulls in Queensland’s Hostplus Cup. As well as the winning field goal, he also chalked up three vital try assists, showing great vision with his passing game. “It’s a special moment, but I've done the work of training, I back my skill to ice that moment, so it's good that it came off like that,” Harrison said. “I'd just say my preparation probably, reps at training … my hard work (helped me get the confidence). “If you nail your prep at training, then you fall back onto that in tough moments like that. “I actually wanted (the ball) at the left post, but we got to the right and it's actually a wrong side for a right-foot kicker, but you get put in those situations as a halfback and you need to step up in big moments and ice those things. “I was always thinking one-pointer when we got in that position and it was just about icing it.” Blooded in Round 10 by Josh Hannay, Harrison has been impressing his coach with his confidence and composure since making the step up into the NRL. "It is easy for us to say, but we see that kid every day train and prepare with composure,” Hannay said after the match. "We do opposed sessions against each and everything we have seen from that kid since day one at pre-season is that composure that you saw tonight. "It is one thing to do it at training, another to do it in front of 20,000 against the Panthers. "The try assists, the field goal ... I feel funny saying this, but it doesn't surprise us. He is the real deal that kid. “That will go in the scrap book for sure but he is going to have a lot of those moments. He's a really measured, smart young person. He wants it. He wants it badly. “He wants to be really good. He was kicking field goals at training yesterday and preparing for that moment. “It doesn't just happen. The good ones prepare for those moments." Harrison said the faith put in him by his coach had helped not only him but his fellow relative newcomers to the top stage, with Hannay debuting a number of young players already this season. “He's been honest with me and I had conversations with him weekly,” Harrison said. “He's been really good with us and not just me, all the young boys, the whole team, his communication is outstanding. “I can't rate him high enough as a coach, so full credit to Josh.” Next up, the Titans will be back at home against the Bulldogs, who similarly had a thrilling one-point win against the Sea Eagles. “We've had a lot of lessons along the way at the moment, but now it's about focusing ahead for Friday night against the Bulldogs back here in front of our Titans fans,” Harrison said. “We want to go back-to-back and we want to win games at the end of the day, so we'll get back to training, we'll get back to working hard again and we'll play the Bulldogs and hopefully get the result.” Venue:

title: Live: World Cup 2026: Ecuador v Curacao updates - RTE.ie
content:
We can probably imagine the scenes in Ecuador right now. Pens are being flung across studio floors in Quito and Guayaquil. The Ecuadorian Tommy Eglington is being name-checked, his honour having been impugned. 'Bring them home' headlines will be emblazoned across the newspapers tomorrow. They are held to a goalless draw by a "boulder in the sea." Meanwhile, the Curacao players are doing a lap of honour in front of their supporters. A historic moment for the tiny island (population: 158,000) which was known as the Dutch Antilles until 2010. "A boulder in the sea has a point at the World Cup!" cries the commentator. Dick Advocaat, his eyes looking slightly glazed and emotional, applauds his players as they secure a historic and remarkable goalless draw against Ecuador. Their goalkeeper Room is the hero, his save tally well into the double digits. At the other end, Curacao even had a couple of chances to snatch it on the counter. Up in the stands at the Arrowhead, the Ecaudorian fans look shell-shocked. An Ecuadorian cross clips off the top of the crossbar Huge dramaa here as Valencia goes to ground in the box. The ref waves it away and VAR agrees with the call. Flicker of a half chance on the break for Curacao. Gorre almost slips in Kasteneer inside the box but the ball squirts under the boot of the attacker. Ecuador have five minutes of injury-time to rustle up a winner. Ireland know from Lisbon last October that this is often the moment when the goal finally arrives. Oooh! Substitute Preciado's miscued cross clips off the top of the crossbar and out for a goal-kick, much to the relief of Curacao. Curacao's occasional counters - which almost yielded a goal on a couple of occasions - becoming increasingly sporadic as they sit back deep in sight of the finish line. A historic draw is a few moments away. There shouldn't be too much injury-time here either. Rueful smiles among the Ecuadorian supporters as another opportunity - possibly their best yet - slips by. Valencia was slipped in by a slick through ball. On first glance, we wondered how he could have side-footed wide of the near post. On the replay, Brenet stuck out a leg and nipped the ball away as Valencia was about to pull the trigger. Better again, the ball ricocheted off the Ecuadorian and out for a goal kick. For the second time in the half, an Ecuadorian corner is halted as the decision is changed - correctly - to goal-kick. An air of frustration and anxiety among the huge Ecuadorian crowd in the Arrowhead as we enter the final eight or nine minutes of normal time. © RTÉ 2026. The Black Caps need five wickets on the final day to claim victory in the second test against England at The Oval – their opponents need a world record. Chasing 463 for victory, the hosts reached the close of play at 182-5, still 281 runs away from victory, as New
Zealand look to square the series ledger at 1-1 before next week’s finale in Nottingham. Once the second innings was wrapped up for 362, courtesy of Henry Nicholls’ day-three century, New Zealand’s bowlers took out the top order to put the Black Caps on course to repeat the heroics of the 1999 side, who claimed an 83-run triumph at the same venue to seal a test series win on English soil more than 20 years ago. Kyle Jamieson has been New Zealand’s standout, taking 3-37 to lead the bowling unit into the final day. The 31-year-old was excellent with both the new and older ball, and used his height exceptionally to trouble England’s top order. He was ably supported by Matt Henry, who deserved far more than the 1-26 he left the field with, while Will O’Rourke chipped in with 1-48. A 97-run partnership between interim captain Joe Root (75 not out) and vice-captain Harry Brook (58) saw England at the very least avoid defeat inside four days, but the hosts do still have a mountain to climb, and an inexperienced lower order left to climb it. Having become only the second player in history to pass 14,000 test runs, Root remains England’s last hope of pulling off something special. He’ll be joined by debutant Jordan Cox (zero not out), but after that, England’s long tail will have a lot of work to do if they’re to do the unthinkable. Resuming at 252-3, the Black Caps’ hopes of a declaration were halted by England taking the remaining seven wickets to wrap the innings up shortly after lunch. Nicholls (121) added just two to his overnight score before he edged to slip, while Tom Blundell (16) and Glenn Phillips (3) couldn’t replicate their first innings displays, caught behind and at gully respectively. Daryl Mitchell should have been gone without adding to the 32 he made late on day three when he was put down by Brook at slip on the first ball of the day, but made the most of that life. From just 68 balls, Mitchell hit six boundaries and one six to raise his 16th test half-century, raised with a reverse-swept four off Root. Once he fell for 68, attempting to scoop Matt Fisher (3-58), New Zealand’s innings went from 349-6 to 362 all out in the hunt for quick runs, as a brisk 38 off 51 balls to Nathan Smith was the only other score of note, leaving England a maximum of 168 overs to score 463 for victory. After struggling with the ball in the first innings, Jamieson knocked the top off England’s chase. First, he had Emilio Gay (11) caught at midwicket by Rachin Ravindra, before trapping Jacob Bethell LBW four balls later for a duck. And while Ben Duckett (9) saw off Jamieson and Henry’s new ball spells, O’Rourke’s introduction saw him miscue a pull shot straight to midwicket to leave England 40-3. As England’s last batting pair of any seniority, Root and Brook staved off New Zealand’s bowlers to reach tea without further loss, before counter-attacking in the evening with a rapid half-century stand, raised in 42 balls. Brook led the charge, and raised the fastest 50 of his test career, needing just 33 deliveries to raise his bat, while Root was more circumspect at the other end and needed 81 balls for his milestone. Henry appeared to remove both LBW, only for reviews to find inside edges to save Brook and then Root. Henry’s persistence was rewarded with the wicket of Brook, excellently caught at slip by Mitchell after a deflection off Blundell’s glove, to expose England’s inexperienced lower order. After struggling with the gloves, dropping several catches and conceding 31 byes across both innings, James Rew’s torrid debut ended in the final 10 minutes of the day, when Jamieson trapped him LBW for 15 with a ball that kept low, after the umpire’s not out decision was overturned. How the players rated in the Hurricanes’ 60-5 win over the Chiefs in Wellington. Scrummaged well and threw himself into everything in open play. His work rate to get around the park and hit rucks was outstanding, while he made a couple
of nice passes and had some good carries. Seemed to have a target set on Damian McKenzie with a couple of solid tackles and running over the top of the Chiefs 10. Rampaging run in build-up to Callum Harkin try. Played his role well with some dominant tackles and hit the ruck with intent. He was strong at the set piece and carried well. Happy to take a few carries to settle things down when play got a bit frantic, made a heap of tackles and did some good work at the breakdown. He also put in a couple of surprisingly lovely kicks, but you know things are getting out of hand when the lock is attempting a cross-field kick to the winger. Rattled the Chiefs by putting pressure on their box kicks and lineout, and was a constant presence in the collision areas. He charged down kicks, took plenty of carries and disrupted the opposition throw. At this point halfbacks and hookers must hate to see him on a team sheet. Back into the starting side after returning from injury via the bench last week, Flanders was at his barnstorming best with ball in hand. He challenged the line early, before charging onto a perfect pass from Proctor to score a try in the second half. Got through plenty of work in a 55-minute shift. He was active at the breakdown and in cleaning out the ruck, made plenty of tackles and took some tough carries into the teeth of the Chiefs’ defence. This is the sort of performance we’ve become accustomed to seeing from Kirifi. Made some big defensive plays to hold Ollie Norris up over the line and recover to pick off a Samipeni Finau pass. He was damaging when he carried the ball into the Chiefs’ defensive line, which he did often. Had an issue or two with the wind early, but worked things out and began to use his kicking game smartly. He did not attack the line with ball in hand too often, but kept things moving nicely as the Hurricanes blew the Chiefs away early and had a couple of assists. Controlled the game nicely and made good decisions throughout, while showing his finishing ability with footwork to leave Liam Coombes-Fabling clutching at air to score, before a diving finish in the corner in the second half. Named man of the match, he completely upstaged McKenzie and left no doubt that he’s ready for an opportunity to steer the ship at test level. Finally broke the single-season individual try-scoring record. Fineanganofo made the most of his chances with ball in hand and made no mistake with the try line in sight. A strong way to finish the campaign for the season’s breakout star. You want your best players to stand up in big games, and Barrett towered over this one. Good touches early and great hustle to charge down an attempted McKenzie clearance early. Broke the line, kept the ball alive for Harkin try. Seemed to have a hand in everything the Hurricanes were doing and was rewarded with a try in the second half. Best player on the pitch. A solid all-around performance. Proctor had some crucial touches in the lead-up to tries and while he conceded a few turnovers, he also did some good work defensively. The All Blacks No 13 jersey seems hotly contested, but a Hurricanes 12-13 combo could certainly have some appeal. Scored two tries to tie Fineanganofo for the try-scoring record. Moorby had plenty of impact with ball in hand, beating defenders and making well over 100m. A call into the All Blacks’ squad would certainly not surprise after the season he’s had. Bonus point for his work holding the ball on the kicking tee. He had a nice run and pass to put Fineanganofo away, showed strength to hold Norris up over the line, showed great hands to pick off a McKenzie pass close to his own line, then was on the spot for a Barrett offload and a try. The quiet contributor of the Hurricanes’ backline, Harkin has been steady all season whether it’s been with 10 or 15 on his back and this was more of the same – maybe even his best performance of the year. Aumua is a hard act to follow, especially in the sort of form he was in for the final, but Devery was solid albeit with limited opportunities. Played the last 22 minutes and gave a good account of himself, particularly on the defensive end. Came into the contest for the final 30 minutes and was solid in his core areas, though missed a few tackles. A solid shift off the bench for the only member of the team to have been a part of the 2016 title-winning run as well. Got stuck into his work in the collision areas and on defence with plenty of tackles, while he also got involved in the attack to set up a try. Made a bunch of tackles and the attack didn’t slow down when he replaced Roigard in the 64th minute. Had a few good carries, forced a turnover and scored a smartly taken try in a busy 12-minute cameo. He became a real asset off the bench for the Hurricanes in the back half of the season and continued in that trend in the final. Maintained a high work rate on both sides of the ball. While the Chiefs’ scrum struggled at times, he was up to the challenge head-to-head against Tosi, and he was among his side’s leading tacklers. Had some issues at set pieces with a lineout disrupted and failed to hook a scrum feed which ultimately led to a messy turnover. In open play, he was strong with ball in hand and he got around the park well to try and make an impact at the ruck. Had a mixed bag defensively as he got over the breakdown to force a penalty but missed a couple of tackles. Held his ground at the scrum, but exited after 22 minutes due to a head knock. Lord was among the hardest workers on the pitch for the Chiefs, leading the game’s tackle count with 20, but did miss a key one on Harkin at the line. He also took a few carries – albeit with little punch behind them – and got in to clean out the ruck. Nothing that will show up on a highlights reel, but some good, honest work. Another early exit, Vaa’i left the game just after halftime after a head knock suffered while making a tackle on Barrett. But even in just 46 minutes, Vaa’i was a busy performer as he tied for a team high in carries with 11 and made double-digit tackles. Pinched a much-needed turnover at the breakdown early and showed some speed as he burst onto the ball to break the line and make plenty of ground - before passing to the other team. He had some good moments, but some forgettable ones in a mixed outing. Got around the ground well and worked hard at the ruck. He was effective at the breakdown early to force a turnover and made plenty of tackles. A busy night defensively with 19 tackles and a turnover and stayed active in the collision areas. He put his hand up for plenty of carries to try and get the side moving in the right direction but was well contained. Was rattled early with a kick charged down and a knock-on in a messy scrum play and never really settled into his work. The tempest swirling in the stadium probably did him no favours but he was far from his best. You hate to see a bloke have a proper stinker in the final, but McKenzie did just that. Three restarts that handed over possession to the Hurricanes, missing touch from a penalty, one charged-down kick and a dropped ball, the veteran couldn’t get anything working for him. Rarely sighted on attack, though made decent ground in his limited opportunities. Taumoefolau had a horrible time on defence trying to contain Moorby and missed some key tackles. Had a lot of traffic come his way and dealt with it for the most part, though may shudder at the thought of having to try to bring down Aumua in full flight again any time soon. Earned a turnover for his side and tried to make something happen with his carrying, though was rarely able to. A muted end to a fantastic individual season. Made little impact in his 50 minutes on the pitch. Seemed the most likely member of the Chiefs backline to spark something and while he made good ground with ball in hand, that didn’t really turn into anything for his side. He was made to work hard defensively, making and missing plenty of tackles. Missed a few tackles, including being left in the dust by Love in the first half. Like Carter, he had some impact with ball in hand but he was limited to just four carries. He made a couple of kicks to try and relieve pressure on his team, but the Hurricanes just kept coming. Played the last 25 minutes and had some impact on the defensive end to force a turnover. Perhaps unlucky not to be awarded a try late in the second half, though Seuseu Naitoa Ah Kuoi crossed a couple of phases later. Played the last 30 minutes with his involvement largely limited to the collision areas. Came into the contest early following Ahio’s injury and while he hit the ruck with intent, he struggled at times at the scrum. Was busy defensively after replacing Vaa’i early in the second half and showed strength to force his way over the tryline late in the contest. Played a 17-minute cameo at the end with limited impact. Entered with 25 minutes left and the game well out of reach, though did assist on his side’s only try. Called upon for the last 30 minutes left and the result a foregone conclusion, yet was still kicking the ball to the opposition. Had a couple of runs but was well contained. Much the same as Jacomb, minus the kicking. Limited impact with ball in hand, but made a few tackles. title: Live: Germany v Ivory Coast - FIFA World Cup - Stuff
content: Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window. This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button. An hour into the game, Germany were getting outplayed by Ivory Coast and trailed by a goal. Coach Julian Nagelsmann needed a spark and substituted in three fresh players, one of whom was Deniz Undav. That decision paid off big time. Undav scored twice as Germany defeated Ivory Coast 2-1 on Sunday (NZ time) and clinched a spot in the knockout phase at the World Cup. “It’s important that everyone sees that even the players from the bench can decide games,” said Undav, who also scored in Germany’s 7-1 opening match rout of Curacao. “Now we have a really important signal to the team. I think that’s very important in a game like this.” Four minutes into stoppage time, Undav received a pass from Felix Nmecha in front of the net and rifled it past Ivory Coast goalkeeper Yahia Fofana to give the Germans a comeback win. It was the German national team’s 11th straight win, a streak dating to September 2025. Undav’s first goal of the match came after Nadiem Amiri sent in a long ball – that striker Kai Havertz let pass him by – onto the boot of Undav, who slammed it into the back of the net in the 68th minute. Both Amiri and Undav had subbed on eight minutes earlier. “Deniz is nobody who needs to be prepared,” Nagelsmann said. “He can jump in right away.” Four-time champions Germany have come back from disappointing group stage exits in 2018 and 2022, while Ivory Coast are still searching for their first knockout stage appearance and could still qualify. The last time Germany got past the group stage they won the tournament in 2014. “Think we showed great character today,” Undav said. “We want to achieve the most.” Ivory Coast captain Franck Kessie opened the scoring in the 30th minute after midfielder Yan Diomande sent in a cross to forward Amad Diallo. His shot was blocked by Germany’s Nathaniel Brown, but the ball bounced back to Kessie, who slotted it in the wide-open left corner of the net. Germany had two goals waved off in a frustrating first half. The first was in the 21st minute when Fofana batted the ball into his own net, but Germany midfielder Aleksander Pavlovic made illegal contact with Fofana on the play. The second came in the 38th minute on a foul, as Jamal Musiala was called for contact on the build-up to what would’ve been a Havertz goal. After a court fight to get into Canada, Elye Wahi, the Ivory Coast striker under investigation for alleged betting-related offences while playing in France for Nice, did not play. title: World Cup: Cody Gakpo scores twice as Reds meet in Netherlands v Sweden - Liverpool FC
content:
Cody Gakpo starred with two goals and an assist as the Netherlands beat Sweden 5-1 at the World Cup on Saturday. Four Liverpool players began the Group F clash in Houston. Gakpo, Ryan Gravenberch and Virgil van Dijk represented the Dutch against Alexander Isak in opposition. Gakpo’s precise low cross created a fifth-minute opener for Brian Brobbey, who soon doubled his nation’s lead from close range. The Reds forward added a third for the Netherlands early in the second half by nudging in Denzel Dumfries’ delivery from yards out. And Gakpo then bagged his second on 55 minutes, moving in from the left corner of the area and clinically dispatching the ball inside the near post. In response, Isak supplied an assist with a through ball for Anthony Elanga to strike a consolation prior to the hour mark. Crysencio Summerville restored a four-goal cushion on the scoreline with a crisp hit from 20 yards near the end. title: Northampton Saints v Exeter Chiefs: Five takeaways as PREM Rugby Final delivers much-needed 'riposte - Planet Rugby
content: George Furbank and Northampton Saints celebrate with PREM Rugby trophy. A sold-out Twickenham, a captain’s farewell written in gold, and a PREM Rugby final that swapped polish for passion and was richer for the trade. Our five takeaways from Northampton Saints v Exeter Chiefs. Before a tackle was logged or a lineout lost, this final had already won something. A crowd of 81,126 filled every tier of Allianz Stadium, two enormous travelling supports painting the bowl in their colours and roaring from first whistle to last. The pre-match did its job too, the American ring announcer David Diamante summoning the sides onto the turf in that unmistakable growl, a new trophy twice the weight of the old one carried out to set the tone, a fanzone humming all afternoon outside. English club rugby has spent recent seasons defending its very existence against a backdrop of financial gloom, so a packed house at headquarters bellowing two well-matched teams into a showpiece is the riposte the game needed. Whatever the 80 minutes delivered, the occasion delivered first. This is a competition learning to sell its spectacle again, and on this evidence the appetite is enormous. The day belonged to PREM Rugby before it belonged to anyone in black, green and gold. Here was the contest in two words; Northampton played as Artists, painting in fast, ambitious strokes, and the numbers leave no argument about who owned the canvas. 58 per cent of possession across the match and 64 in the second half, 107 rucks to 61, a flawless 100 per cent off their own lineout. Player of the Match Henry Pollock carried 16 times and beat eight defenders, whilst Tommy Freeman made two clean breaks and a game-high 81 metres, and Fin Smith ran the whole thing with a conductor’s calm and a brilliant kick strategy. Smith was arguably the finest player on the field by a distance, his kicking from hand a masterclass in territory and shape, two turnovers won at the other end, and a try of his own on the half-hour to crown it. Northampton player ratings: Henry Pollock haters humbled as ‘ferocious’ star delivers ‘trademark’ performance and bench provides ‘bulletproof’ defence Exeter answered as Artisans, craftsmen of the unglamorous, and their currency was the tackle and their huge belief and power. They made 183 of them to Northampton’s 101, a number that tells you everything about how the afternoon felt for them, a side hanging on by its fingernails and refusing to let go. For long stretches Saints could not find their finish. Pollock was held up over the line, 12 phases on the Exeter five yielded nothing, and Campbell Ridl produced a miracle to deny Alex Mitchell when a try looked certain. The masterpiece sat unfinished and the inquest loomed. Then, with the game crying out for an end product, Northampton found it, George Hendy crossing twice in the corner to settle it. The Artists did it, and Northampton, in the end, framed their own work. Spare a long look at the Chiefs, because defeat does no justice to their journey. 12 months ago this was a ninth-placed side searching for an identity. Rob Baxter has rebuilt them into a team that finished third, exhumed itself from 16 down to bury the champions Bath at the Rec, and then walked into a sold-out Twickenham and led the final with half an hour to play. The defiance was everywhere today; Ethan Roots, back from concussion, flattened Smith with a hit that nearly took the roof off. Greg Fisilau and Len Ikitau hammered the gain line all afternoon, and Ikitau even poached a turnover for good measure. Ridl’s try-saving tackle was the single image of their resistance, the soul of the side in one act. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The craft came from Stephen Varney, the scrum-half supplying the only sustained quality in blue, an exquisite 50:22 from his own half to win a foothold and the sumptuous pass that sent skipper Dafydd Jenkins over for the lead. The one thing that broke them was the set piece, a lineout that returned a wretched 60 per cent and was raided again and again by Alex Coles and Ed Prowse. Win that ball cleanly and Exeter might have turned their pressure into a very different scoreline. They could not, and it cost them. Even so, Baxter walks away with a young spine, a clear identity and a platform that points upward and there’s little doubt the Chiefs are on the rise. Two factors decided a tight final; the first was depth. Phil Dowson loaded his bench six-two for exactly the closing quarter that wins finals, and it paid in full. JJ van der Mescht thundered on and lifted the carry, Callum Chick raised the physical level, and the prop Danilo Fischetti jackaled turnovers like a flanker. Fresh power against emptied legs is a one-way street, and Northampton’s 64 per cent second-half possession was the dividend of having more to give when it mattered. Exeter Chiefs player ratings: Yellow card ‘costly’ for Devonians while ‘fantastic signing’ enjoys ‘showstopper’ in final The second was discipline, and it swung twice. Josh Kemeny went to the bin for a head shot on Jenkins, and while Saints were down to fourteen, Exeter struck for the Jenkins try and the lead. The pendulum then swung straight back. Jenkins himself was yellow-carded for a high hit on Furbank, the sanction kept to 10 minutes by the mitigation of the full-back dropping into the contact, and in the Exeter captain’s absence Northampton scored both of Hendy’s tries to take the game away. The cards were the hinge, and Exeter’s came at the fatal hour. A word, too, for Matthew Carley, who refereed with feel and courage all afternoon, the Jenkins mitigation and a late rugby-incident call on an accidental head clash both spot on. He swore in the build-up that you have to earn your fairytale and George Furbank earned his. Man and boy at this club, he came through the academy in 2016 and made his senior debut against, of all sides, Exeter, marking it with a try. 10 seasons on, he led Saints out at a packed Twickenham one last time before Harlequins, and signed off with the trophy in his hands, 68 metres made and a clean break on the day for good measure. The numbers frame a one-club life, more than 140 appearances, 283 points, a Prem title in 2023/24, the 66th captaincy in the club’s history and 14 England caps. The farewell tour was nearly stolen from him by arm, concussion, calf and knee trouble that limited him to a handful of games across two dark seasons. He got the ending he had been denied all that time. So the bow on a wild afternoon. This was short on accuracy, heavy on errors, the lineouts ragged and the chances spurned by the bucketload. It was also overflowing with heart, the kind of final that sends people home hoarse and happy. Just desserts for Northampton, the better side across 80 minutes and deserving champions. Deep respect to Exeter, whose rebuild and refusal lit up the contest. A great final in every aspect that matters. The skill came and went, but the passion remained; what a game! title: What TV channel is Germany v Ivory Coast on tonight? Kick-off time and live stream - Wales Online
content: Players of Germany celebrate after their team's seventh goal against Curacao(Image: Sebastian Widmann - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images) Germany and Ivory Coast lock horns tonight in the teams' second match in Group E at the World Cup. The result was expected, of course, with the tiny CONCACAF nation boasting a population of just over 150,000. title: Barbarians player ratings v Springboks: 'Incredibly annoying' All Blacks great has flashes of brilliance as Scott Robertson's side are 'outclassed' - Planet Rugby
content: TJ Perenara and an inset of Warrick Gelant Following an entertaining 80-31 defeat to the Springboks, here is how we rated Scott Robertson’s Barbarians at the Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium. 15 Warrick Gelant: A great long pass led to Andrew Kellaway’s first try as the Springbok full-back attempted to weave his magic whenever he touched the ball. He made two line breaks and threatened his fellow countrymen’s defence but also missed four tackles, struggled under the high ball and conceded possession twice. 6 14 Andrew Kellaway: Made four carries and scored two tries, hardly a poor return, but the snubbed Wallabies back was regularly beaten in the air and on the ground by the brilliant Edwill van der Merwe. 5 13 Virimi Vakatawa: A joy to watch as per usual. The former French international brilliantly skinned Cheslin Kolbe en route to his try and assisted another. Sure, he was caught out often in defence with the Baa-Baas backtracking, but he certainly embraced the spirit of the invitational team. 7 12 Alex Nankivell: Superbly skipped past Quan Horn and linked up with his midfield partner to set up the first Barbarians’ try. He made some good metres through that channel and defended bravely. 6 11 Duhan van der Merwe: Chopped down by Siya Kolisi near the try-line early when he looked threatening but hit back with a great scramble defence cover tackle on Kolbe. Like Kellaway, he struggled under the high ball but did make some good ground with ball in hand. 5 10 Tomás Albornoz: Always looking to create and did so with some success as he proved to be a great half-back partner for TJ Perenara. His clearance in the first minute of the game was simply superb. The Argentine was good value for 55 minutes and showed why he is one of the best number 10s in the business. 7 9 TJ Perenara (c): It’s a good thing that Robertson made the former All Black captain or else he would have certainly been carded for his constant complaining in the referee’s ear. He did visit the bin for a poor upright tackle on Riley Norton in the 13th minute but returned to score a stunning try before half-time. That period before the break was perhaps the Baa-Baas’ best and Perenara was central throughout. Incredibly annoying but still world-class. 7 Springboks player ratings: Cheslin Kolbe’s mixed bag, Junior Bok captain shines as Edwill van der Merwe scores three 8 Miracle Fai’ilagi: Flattened Kolbe, a real size mismatch, and beat the Springboks winger soon after. He made a fantastic cover tackle on Siya Kolisi but failed to roll away and was deemed to have been cynical and spent 10 minutes in the sin bin. The Moana Pasifika captain was one of the few Barbarians who really muscled up to the Boks’ physicality. 7 7 Lachlan Boshier: The top tackler in the match but that took its toll on the ex-Chiefs back-rower, who was shunted to the ground by Andre Esterhuizen in the latter stages. 6 6 Guido Petti: A busy shift from the Los Pumas forward who contested well in the lineouts, cleared out rucks and toiled with the Bok pack reasonably well for 75 minutes. 6 5 Izack Rodda: Ditto for the former Wallaby who played 53 minutes before trotting to the sidelines. He was part of a pack that was largely overpowered. 6 Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. 4 Franco Molina: The Baas-Baas did manage to cause some troubles for the Boks’ lineout and much of the credit lies with Molina for that. The Los Puma was relentless in the tight too. 7 3 D’Arcy Rae: Battered in the scrum, an area the Barbarians were never really going to have a chance. Rather anonymous in the loose too. title: Springboks v Barbarians: Five takeaways as Rassie Erasmus experiments have mixed success - Planet Rugby
content: Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus and wing Cheslin Kolbe. Following an 80-31 victory for the Springboks over the Barbarians on Saturday, here’s our five takeaways from the clash at the Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium. The Springboks overcame a slack six minutes to dominate the Barbarians in the second period and open their international season with a dominant victory. In typical Baa-Baas style, there was plenty of free-flowing rugby – from both sides – but South Africa’s success came from them doubling down on their super strengths, namely their scrum and maul. Rassie Erasmus’ men played some excellent rugby early on, going 35-7 in front thanks to Edwill van der Merwe’s double and further tries from Pieter-Steph du Toit, Jasper Wiese and Riley Norton – three of those coming after TJ Perenara and Miracle Fai’ilagi had been sin-binned. However, a yellow card of their own for Grant Williams enabled the invitational team to hit back with Franco Molina, Andrew Kellaway and Perenara adding to Virimi Vakatawa’s earlier try to reduce the arrears. That was as good as it got for the visitors, whose week on the lash caught up with them in the second period. Cheslin Kolbe crossed the whitewash at the end of the first half and they then proceeded to score 40 more points after the break. Van der Merwe completed his hat-trick while JJ Kotze, Faf de Klerk, Jesse Kriel, Andre Esterhuizen and Zach Porthen also went over to complete the rout. Erasmus will be looking for the successors to the likes of Siya Kolisi, Du Toit and perhaps even Wiese post-Rugby World Cup, but right now they remain their first choice back-row and it is easy to see why. Wiese, having spent another season in Asia in the slightly less taxing Japan Rugby League One, looked fit and sharp and was barrelling over established internationals with regularity, even at close quarters. Du Toit and Kolisi were playing slightly wider, as has often been the way since the arrival of Tony Brown, and they thrived in those spaces. It was the skipper who provided the assist for Van der Merwe’s first try with a deft pass after drawing the final defender, while his flank team-mate proved incredibly difficult to stop when probing that five-metre channel on the wing. Du Toit was also rewarded for his performance by going over the line, although it came via the more direct route with a powerful surge close to the whitewash. The trio were also among their top-tacklers, although the two-time World Rugby Player of the Year did miss a few, so there is still plenty to work on after they managed to blow off the cobwebs ahead of the England clash. The strength of the squad on Saturday may have taken a few by surprise but, as Erasmus stated, it is acting as preparation for their huge Test against the English in the Nations Championship. However, that did not prevent the Boks from trialling a few things, which included a new fly-half and second-row forward. Quan Horn, who has never started at 10 for the Lions, was handed the role in what was a fascinating move from the hosts. He has a fine passing game and a hefty left boot, and those two facets were in evidence on occasion, but his inexperience generally showed. Horn did not quite know where to stand, made a few poor decisions and ultimately needs plenty of work if he is to be comfortable going forward. Equally, he will be frustrated by his early defensive work after being run over by Alex Nankivell for Vakatawa’s score. His selection also left them without what most consider an out-and-out goal-kicker, certainly at international level, but it is a responsibility Cheslin Kolbe has taken on in Japan to great success. Kolbe has been operating at 81 per cent and the wing was handed the role against the Barbarians, where he was exceptional, kicking nine conversions. One of those kicks came after Norton touched down, the U20 captain who has yet to play a professional game for the Stormers. The youngster is very highly regarded in South Africa, and those talents were evident from the start. What was particularly noticeable was his technical work in the tight, which belied his tender years, while he did not shirk anything physically. Impressive from the lock, who looks destined to have a long Springboks career. Springboks player ratings: Cheslin Kolbe’s mixed bag, Junior Bok captain shines as Edwill van der Merwe scores three After the disappointing contest last year, neutrals were hoping for a better display in 2026 from what was, on paper at least, a talented side, but when they lost Perenara and Fai’ilagi to the sin bin and shipped three tries in that period, it did not look promising. It left them 35-7 in arrears and facing an embarrassing afternoon at the Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium, but the Boks also struggled to keep their discipline. Scrum-half Williams was yellow-carded for a deliberate knock-on, and during those 10 minutes, the Baa-Baas played some spellbinding rugby as they also touched down three times. Erasmus would have been concerned by their midfield defence with Andre Esterhuizen and Jesse Kriel biting in, giving too much space on the outside. Those two experienced centres perhaps wanted to offer a helping hand to the fly-half, who was run over by Nankivell early on, but those gaps were exploited by the invitational side at the end of the first half. However, the Barbarians were unable to maintain that momentum and a needless mistake from the restart enabled Kolbe to cross the whitewash while South Africa were down to 14 to ease the pressure going into the second period. They would then keep their foot on the throat after the break, despite an early yellow card for Aphelele Fassi. The Springboks went back to basics and were much more direct, going to their trusty maul and scrum, and duly bullied the visitors physically in the final 35 minutes. Barbarians player ratings v Springboks: ‘Incredibly annoying’ All Blacks great has flashes of brilliance as Scott Robertson’s side are ‘outclassed’ In many ways, we enjoyed TJ Perenara’s combative approach. Sometimes these games can be a bit of a jolly for those Barbarians players, but Perenara, having been given the opportunity to face South Africa for the first time since 2024, was clearly desperate to win. The former All Blacks scrum-half, to his immense credit, was everywhere both with and without the ball, but that sheer competitiveness spilled over to disrespect towards the referee. He had already been sin-binned for a high shot but, after returning to the field, Perenara did not stop moaning at the man in the middle. Morné Ferreira attempted to calm him down, warning him about his behaviour and even calling him a “legend of the game”, perhaps trying to appeal to his ego, but quite frankly he would have been better served simply penalising him and, if he continued, giving him a second yellow. Given that these games are the friendliest of friendlies, Ferreira understandably didn’t want to do that, but Perenara’s attitude was simply unacceptable and should have been sanctioned. title: France XV v England XV: Winners and losers as Les Bleus flex 'riches' in glorified training run - Planet Rugby
content: France's Nolan Le Garrec and an inset of England's George Ford. France XV beat England XV 35-19 at a sun-drenched Stade de la Rabine on Friday, a five-try evening that flattered England only in the sense that it could comfortably have been worse. Bordeaux’s rising star Marko Gazzotti was imperious at the base at eight, Nolann Le Garrec marked an emotional return to the Vannes club that made him, and an England side shorn of its first-choice spine came apart the moment the benches emptied. The lasting image was Benhard Janse van Rensburg dropping the ball over the line with nobody within ten yards of him, two days before Steve Borthwick must name a Nations Championship squad. Bordeaux’s early Top 14 exit was supposed to be the great inconvenience of France’s summer, depriving Fabien Galthie of his champions for the southern tour. On this evidence it simply handed his second string a spine of genuine quality, and Gazzotti was the heartbeat of it. The number eight carried with huge impact every time he touched the ball, linked midfield to forward play with the ease of a man who has been doing it in European finals, and gave Le Garrec a platform so clean that France’s attack purred from the first quarter. He was the best forward on the pitch by a distance, and he barely had to leave second gear to prove it. France have a problem in the back-row of their scrum only in the sense that they now have too many good options. This was Le Garrec’s night before a ball was kicked. Formed at Vannes, he had somehow never played a competitive match at La Rabine, and the emotion of hearing the Marseillaise sung back at him by the people who first watched him was written all over his face. He answered it in the perfect way, sniping over for the third try midway through the second half before departing four minutes later to a standing ovation he had earned ten years in advance. What followed showed France’s strength in the position, because Baptiste Jauneau arrived from the bench and kept the tempo exactly where his predecessor had left it. His quick tap-and-go for the fifth try, taken while all 15 England players stood admiring the scenery, was the work of a scrum-half who had read the game’s complacency long before the men in white did. For all France’s riches, the depth of their front-row has nagged at Galthie for two seasons. He will have driven home from Brittany rather happier on that score. Jefferson Poirot, recalled at 33 and six years on from walking away from international rugby, anchored the loosehead with the calm of a man who never really left, and when Régis Montagne came on around the three-quarter mark the French scrum lifted from solid to overwhelming. Throw in six uncapped players blooded without the result ever wobbling, and a coach who came to experiment leaves with a clutch of answers. The set-piece that broke England in the final quarter was assembled almost entirely from reserves. France XV v England XV: Five takeaways as Benhard Janse van Rensburg blows ‘golden chance’ as ‘error strewn’ visitors give Steve Borthwick food for thought If Gazzotti supplied the platform, Hastoy supplied the control. The fly-half was faultless off the tee in glorious kicking conditions, threaded the pass that sent Nicolas Depoortere over for the opening French try on the counter, and helped himself to a score of his own in the 51st minute that effectively closed the contest at 28-12. He managed the game with the authority of someone who knew his pack was winning the collisions, and he asked questions of England’s spacing that his opposite number never came close to asking in return. Yoram Moefana and Depoortere gave France a centre pairing of real craft and vision. Truth be known, they are probably France’s number one pairing but Galthie has so many options now. Moefana’s inside ball, a gorgeous renversement that wrong-footed the entire England line, sent Grégoire Arfeuil scorching clear for the second try and was the single most creative moment of the half. Depoortere, back in the blue of France, marked his return with the opening score and looked every inch a Test 13. England spent the night chasing shadows in the wide channels, and these two were the reason. The clearest sign of France’s depth was that their bench did not dilute the performance; it intensified it. Tixeront was central to that, thundering off the pine to add fresh legs and fresh menace to a back-row that already had England wilting. He carried hard, hunted at the breakdown and helped tip the contest from competitive to one-sided in the third quarter, the kind of cameo that turns a squad member into a tour selection. When your replacements raise the level rather than protect it, you are a side in rude health. The captain’s armband demanded a performance of control and direction, and Ford delivered flashes of the former and almost none of the latter. There were the familiar lovely touches, the odd flat pass that promised something, but for 80 minutes he could not get his backline moving or his carriers over the gainline with any rhythm. England’s most creative passages arrived in spite of their structure rather than because of it, and a fly-half of his experience leading a side this disjointed has to wear that. He set up Max Ojomoh’s late consolation, and on another night that might soften the verdict. On this one it merely underlined how little had come before it. Alex Dombrandt, Tom Curry and Ted Hill spent the evening looking like carthorses in a sweat, laboured and a yard off the pace against a French unit that moved through the gears at will. The tackle counts will flatter them, Dombrandt’s especially, but a tackle count is what you rack up when the opposition has the ball and the territory, and France had both for long stretches. Curry’s effort on his return from a grade-three calf tear was honest, yet honesty was never the problem. Breakdown speed, carry threat and the ability to live with a quicker, sharper back-row all were, and England were second best in every one of them. England XV player ratings: Cadan Murley ‘pushes his case’ for Springboks Test as Noah Caluori ‘not out of place’ The starting trio held their own early, and Asher Opoku-Fordjour did his loosehead credentials no harm. The damage came when the bench emptied. From that point England’s scrum was overpowered, shoved backwards, penalised and ultimately demoralised by a French unit running on reserves. The retreat bled into the rest of the side, concentration drained, and by the time Fabien Brau-Boirie sauntered in untouched there was not an English head still in the game. Our own ratings were generous to a fault here. A scrum that goes into reverse against a scratch French pack is not a six-out-of-ten afternoon, however willing the effort. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The fixture was sold on a single promise, that it would be free and available to all, the modern game reaching out to its audience. The platform then spent the evening betraying that promise. Buffering at the worst possible moments, a picture that dipped to a quality you would have been embarrassed by a decade ago, and a viewing experience that turned a simple watch into a test of patience. If you make accessibility the entire pitch, the least required is a stream that holds its shape for 80 minutes. This one did not come close, and on a night when the rugby offered little, the people who tuned in for free deserved a great deal better. Here is the uncomfortable truth beneath all five tries. This was a game without a single thing riding on it, no caps, no jeopardy, no trophy, no consequence, dropped into a weekend already groaning under a URC final and the business end of the Top 14. 30-odd professionals were asked to put their bodies on the line in a contest history will not record, while the real drama of the season played out elsewhere. Janse van Rensburg’s fumble became the emblem of the whole exercise, a young man desperate to matter in a match that did not. You can dress these run-outs up as preparation, and the coaches duly did, but a glorified opposed session in front of 12,000 curious locals is a strange use of a summer Friday. The question worth asking is not how England played, it is why anyone signed this off in the first place? title: World Cup schedule today: How to watch Netherlands v Sweden, TV channels & live stream Saturday 20 June - The Guardian
content: Live blog: the latest news from around the tournament Group F is shaping up to be one of the most competitive at the 2026 World Cup with Japan, the Netherlands and Sweden all talented enough to make a deep run. The second round of group games could reveal whether or not that is realistic. The stakes are high. Japan and the Netherlands started their World Cup campaigns by sharing the spoils, but both teams could do with a win in their second game to be sure of their place in the last 32. They may have to demonstrate more ambition than they did in their opener. Sweden, meanwhile, made a statement by putting five goals past Tunisia. Viktor Gyökeres and Alexander Isak both found the back of the net in a display that made others sit up and take note. Graham Potter’s team are worth watching. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s World Cup games, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options. Ronald Koeman has faced some criticism for the changes he made when the Netherlands were leading against Japan, and many are expecting a more assertive approach against Sweden. Koeman, however, may lack the creative personnel for the Dutch to truly impose their own game. Sweden, on the other hand, demonstrated their attacking threat in a 5-1 win over Tunisia that hinted at a growing understanding between Gyökeres and Isak. If Potter can balance the forward line with the rest of his team, Sweden could be dark horses to make a run. Player to watch: Alexander Isak, Sweden – after he missed so much of his first season at Liverpool with injuries, it was refreshing to see Isak at something close to his best against Tunisia. His direct threat could trouble club teammate Virgil van Dijk. Fortune favours Kamada as Japan rescue World Cup draw with Netherlands Graham Potter: ‘I feel very Swedish when I’m working – I look a bit Swedish’ While Germany put seven goals past Curaçao in their World Cup opener, the standard of the opposition means the true gauge of Julian Nagelsmann’s team is still to be taken. The four-time winners have failed to reach the knockout stage of the last two World Cups, but they are well-placed to end that streak. In overcoming one of Conmebol’s strictest defenses in their opening match against Ecuador, Côte d’Ivoire made a statement of intent even if they needed a late winner. The Elephants have a variety of taking options that could take them far. Player to watch: Yan Diomande, Côte d’Ivoire – the in-demand RB Leipzig winger was relentless against Ecuador, showing why Liverpool and Paris Saint-Germain are reportedly interested in his services. Curaçao enjoy their moment but Havertz and ruthless Germany show no mercy ‘We are knocking on the door’: Africa’s 10 contenders target World Cup glory While Ecuador underwhelmed in their opener against Côte d’Ivoire, the team who finished an impressive second in Conmebol qualifying could still make an impact at this tournament. They must, however, show more attacking intent. Livano Comenencia’s equalizer for Curaçao against Germany was one of the moments of the World Cup so far. While his team ultimately suffered a heavy defeat, their ambition to venture forward when possible should be a warning sign to Ecuador. Player to watch: Moisés Caicedo, Ecuador – the Chelsea midfielder is Ecuador’s valve in the center of the pitch, giving them the ability to hit out on the break. Caicedo will also have to be at his creative best against Curaçao’s low block. Why Ecuador, Japan and Norway are the dark horses at this World Cup ‘Everyone is welcome with us’: Curaçao want you along for their first World Cup ride Tunisia shot themselves in the foot more than once as they opened their World Cup campaign with a 5-1 loss to Sweden – a result so poor they sacked their head coach and appointed Hervé Renard until the end of the tournament. If they can cut out the mistakes, though, they could still salvage their World Cup. Japan could be one of the most adaptable teams at this tournament if their opener against the Netherlands is anything to go by. Hajime Moriyasu knows how to set up his side to sit deep, but also to control games higher up the field. Player to watch: Takefusa Kubo, Japan – while the Real Sociedad playmaker wasn’t at his best against the Netherlands, his ability as a creator could be key to breaking down Tunisia. title: SA 'A' player ratings v Zimbabwe: Future 50-cap Springbok and Lukhanyo Am shine - Planet Rugby
content: South Africa A centres Lukhanyo Am and Markus Muller with an inset of fly-half Yaqeen Ahmed. Following South Africa A’s 40-0 victory over the Zimbabwe Sables, here’s how we rated Mzwandile Stick’s charges at the Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium. 15 Luan Giliomee: Unfazed by anything the Sables threw at him as he remained calm in the backfield and stepped up to run the show at fly-half after Ahmed’s red card. Has been likened to Pat Lambie by many and it’s easy to see why. He has a well-rounded skillset, a calm head and is confident in his execution, all of which was on display today. 8 14 Jaco Williams: Regularly popped up in pockets that troubled the Sables, and it paid off with his snipe around the rucks and delivered a great offload for Imad Khan to score. He also made some sharp defensive reads and contested well in the air. A tidy performance with flashes of brilliance. He punished a poor clearance kick to score, showing that the future of the Springboks wing stocks is in rude health. 8 13 Markus Muller: There is a lot of excitement around the youngest-ever Stormers debutant, and much like many of his teammates today, he didn’t have too many opportunities to really strut his strengths. Still, he showed great anticipation and rugby IQ to grab the second try of the game, pouncing on the loose ball after Siyaya’s hit. Defensively, he worked well in tandem with Am and was largely faultless. 7 12 Lukhanyo Am: The man among the boys in the backline, the World Cup winner was a calming presence and glue-man for SA’A. He mopped up loose balls, carried and defended well too. Had a bit more swagger to his step after looking out of sorts before his move to Japan. In terms of pedigree, Am was the best player on the pitch, and while he wasn’t game-breaking or outrageous, he played like the seasoned professional he is. 8 Springboks v Barbarians: Prediction, players to watch, kick-off time, TV coverage and more 11 Zekhethelo Siyaya: Friendly fire ended a lively performance far too early as he went for an HIA after Emmanuel Tshituka’s massive boot clattered into his face. This after he came close to scoring a hat-trick, denied twice by the TMO, but did land a great hit on Dulan Utete leading to Muller’s try. 7 10 Yaqeen Ahmed: Elegantly glides across the pitch; it really is a delightful sight. He took his try brilliantly with a great dummy and sprint to the try line. Showed real attacking endeavour and made good decisions overall until his chip over the top deep inside Zimbabwe’s 22, when he took Tapiwa Mafura out in the air and rightly sin-binned for his mistake. A red card perhaps a bit harsh considering the actions of Utete but a learning experience for the promising Junior Boks fly-half. 5 9 Haashim Pead: Slick service to the forwards and Ahmed, kicked well and made a lovely break around the fringes to score in the 31st minute. Kept the Sables’ defence on their toes and was replaced at half-time, with Nico Steyn getting a run. What was most promising from a Springboks perspective is just how comfortable he looked in the structures. 7 Springboks legend hits out at URC Final officials for fabricating ‘fiction’ in Bulls’ disallowed tries 8 Phepsi Buthelezi: A busy ball carrier for South Africa A as he was for the Sharks this season. He also showed off his softer skills with some nice tip-on passes. A solid outing for the one-Test Bok. 6 7 Bathobele Hlekani: Hulking carries as he powered through contact time and time again but lacked the service to provide the final pass to Van Heerden in the 24th minute. Still, he was busy and effective in his time on the pitch with good hits on defence too. Did not look out of place for a second before making way for Sibabalwe Mahashe. 8 6 Emmanuel Tshituka: The younger Tshituka brother is now tied to the Springboks, which was another key bonus of this fixture with SA Rugby capturing a plethora of rising talents. Manny is renowned for his work rate in Durban, and it was much of the same again today as he went hunting for work. 7 Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. 5 Ruben van Heerden: The lineout was messy, but that wasn’t all his doing, with Mnebelele’s throws not being up to Test standard yet. Still, the Stormers workhorse threw his weight around into just about everything. Had Hlekani managed to free up his arms better, Van Heerden would have grabbed a try. Nothing really stood out about the lock’s performance, whether it was good or bad. 6 Springboks legends’ verdict on Rassie Erasmus’ shock selection as ‘Andre the Giant’ provides ‘nice release valve’ 4 Vincent Tshituka (c): The SA’A captain brought his back-row energy to his shift in the second-row before moving into the loose trio later in the game. He troubled the Sables’ defence with his ball carries and didn’t shy away from contact in defence. Perhaps not as dominant as the Springboks coaching staff will have wanted, but a strong performance nonetheless. 7 3 Neethling Fouche: Part of a dominant scrummaging effort and did what he does for the Stormers, his job and did it well. Little fuss, little flash, just an effective, efficient performance. 6 2 Siphosethu Mnebelele: The similarities to Bongi Mbonambi are unavoidable. Mnebelele is incredibly abrasive in contact and physically imposes himself on both sides of the ball. He is clearly a strong scrummager, with his real work-on being his lineout throws that weren’t great. The 20-year-old is a real prospect to keep an eye on – he has a 50-cap Springbok written all over him. 7 1 Boan Venter: He will have enjoyed the amount of opportunities he got to stretch his legs with ball in hand and impressed when he did so. Dominant in the scrums too, which was expected, while his handling skills are somewhat underrated. 7 Replacements: Nico Steyn made a lively impact off the bench, kicking well, competing at the breakdown and generally making good decisions as South Africa got a sharp 80 minutes out of their scrum-halves. Imad Khan grabbed a try in his loose backline role while the replacement front-row kept the Springboks’ Bomb Squad tradition of dominating the scrum and making a really positive impact on the whole, with the mauls also coming more to the fore. title: Hurricanes v Chiefs: Five takeaways as Canes enter 'greatest-ever champions' debate after All Blacks ruthlessly punish Damian McKenzie's 'disasterclass' - Planet Rugby
content: Jordie Barrett lifts the Super Rugby Pacific trophy and inset of Damian McKenzie. Following the Hurricanes’ record-breaking 60-5 victory over the Chiefs in the 2026 Super Rugby Pacific Final, here are our five takeaways. It’s been 10 years, but the Hurricanes are Super Rugby champions yet again, humiliating the Chiefs in the 2026 final to clinch just their second title. Nine tries, six conversions and a penalty goal meant that the ‘Canes racked up 60 points in what was a truly dominant thrashing of the second-best club in the tournament this year, who managed just five points in reply. A gulf in class is an understatement as the Hurricanes bossed every single facet of the game with their attack ripping the Chiefs to shreds and their defence ensuring that this one was never in doubt. Josh Moorby got the scoreboard ticking in the fifth minute, and the hosts would lead from then on with Ruben Love following eight minutes later before Fehi Fineanganofo broke the record for the most tries in a second season in the 23rd minute. Callum Harkin scored the fourth and final try of the first half with Love adding the extras and a penalty as the ‘Canes led 29-0 as the two sets of players headed to the sheds. Moorby joined Fineanganofo on 17 tries in 2026 when he crossed for the fifth try of the match just three minutes into the second half, with departing flanker Devan Flanders making it six five-pointers soon after. The Chiefs had no answer for what the Hurricanes threw at them as Jordie Barrett got in on the tries, with Love doubling his tally after the hour-mark. Naitoa Ah Kuoi got one back for the Chiefs, which only ensured that the visitors didn’t end the final with a doughnut, but the champions would have the final say of the match, showpiece and the season with Jone Rova slamming down the exclamation mark on an incredible team performance. Hurricanes end decade-long Super Rugby title wait putting 60 points on Chiefs as All Blacks star Ruben Love dominates Undoubtedly a world-class player, Damian McKenzie produced one of his worst-ever performances in a Chiefs jersey with a truly horrendous first-half showing that hamstrung his team and gifted ascendancy to the Hurricanes time and time again. He butchered three restarts, threw a pass directly into Harkin’s clutches in a threatening attacking position, and was charged down a couple of times. After Moorby grabbed the opener, McKenzie gifted the hosts possession on the halfway line, slamming his restart into the in-goal with no pressure on Harkin, who forced it down for a scrum. Two minutes later, he made another error, missing touch with his penalty kick, again relieving pressure. Not too long after, the Hurricanes were in again through Love with the Chiefs under pressure in their own half. McKenzie further compounded his errors as right after Love’s try, he thumped the restart hard low, and the Hurricanes let it roll over the try line and for another scrum on halfway. With the Chiefs desperately looking to hit back, Norris tucks and carries in centre field, as does Dyer, stopped 18 metres out. McKenzie then drifted into space in the 35th minute but forced the attack and threw his pass straight to Harkin. Two minutes later, Harkin was in for the Canes’ next score, opening up a 26-0 lead. The ensuing restart, McKenzie attempted to go short, the wind caught it and gifted the Hurricanes a scrum again. There they won a penalty, and Love made it 29-0 at the break. Matters didn’t get much better for the All Blacks playmaker in the second half as he was held up in contact, with the Hurricanes awarded another scrum. Moorby doubled his tally after another lovely attacking move from the set-piece. In the 54th minute, McKenzie spilled the ball, undoing all his great cover work in the backfield, and the Hurricanes ruthlessly pounced with Barrett crossing the whitewash. Frankly, as good a player as McKenzie clearly is, tonight was not his night, and the mind boggles as to why the Chiefs’ coaching team did not act and put him out of his misery. Surely it couldn’t get much worse? In the words of Mick McCarthy: ‘It can!’ And it did. So often McKenzie has been the heart-beat, fulcrum of this team, but today he was a hindrance, a liability. Chiefs player ratings: Damian McKenzie produces final ‘horror show’ as several All Blacks stars endure ‘nightmare’ performances The 2009 Bulls. The 2012 Chiefs. The 1996 Blues. The 2018 Crusaders (or just about any of Scott Robertson’s teams). And now the 2026 Hurricanes have entered the conversation. The men from Wellington have waited 10 long years to add a second Super Rugby Pacific title and did so in a manner we have only seen a handful of times in this tournament’s history. Sure, they had their hiccups along the way, losing three regular season matches, but when it came to the crunch, the team that so often collapsed thrived, hammering the ACT Brumbies 66-12, a record score in Super Rugby knockouts. The Blues caused them a bit of trouble for 40 minutes in the semi-final, but once they started changing gears, they cruised to a 57-21 win. Then, they made it a hat-trick of 50+ point performances today with a mesmerizing showing where they completely outplayed the second-best team in the tournament. Tonight was the eighth occasion this season that ‘Canes racked up over 50 points in a match. The next best such tally this season? Four. The numbers behind their season are simply insane. They weren’t just the best points-scoring team during the regular season (562, including 86 tries), but they were also the most astute defence, conceding 298 points and 44 tries. Once they entered the knockout stages, the records continued to tumble, becoming the first team to score 100 tries in a single Super Rugby season, and they absolutely smashed their 2017 record of 97, finishing on 113! After crossing for nine tries in the final, the only issue Clark Laidlaw will have with the performance today was not keeping the Chiefs scoreless, but that won’t keep him sleepless at all as the ‘Canes claimed the biggest-ever Super Rugby final victory. Hurricanes player ratings: Jordie Barrett absolute ‘perfection’ as Ruben Love ‘decides’ All Blacks 10 battle while stunning wings break Super Rugby record New Zealand is never short on classy outside backs and wings in particular, but as Dave Rennie finalises his All Blacks squad ahead of Monday’s team announcement, two names surely have to feature: Fineanganofo and Moorby. The duo were sublime all season to break Joe Roff and Ben Lam’s try records and didn’t slip when it mattered most; in fact, during the play-off stages, they got even better. Moorby offers the benefit of being able to cover full-back too, which could be pivotal during the July Tests with Will Jordan sidelined, but considering how underwhelming the All Blacks’ wingers were as a collective last season, throwing uncapped players into the mix can’t be the worst idea. Fineanganofo’s situation is a bit trickier considering that he signed for the Newcastle Red Bulls before the start of the season, but selecting him in the squad should be non-negotiable. That can spark discussions around getting him out of that contract. The performances of Cam Roigard, Love, Barrett, Harkin, Billy Proctor and so many others made life easier for the free-scoring outside backs both today and throughout this season, but there is still so much value in having wingers who are in red-hot form and ruthlessly take opportunities that come their way. Where are they now? First Hurricanes team to win Super Rugby in 2016 After falling short of European glory with Leinster last season, Barrett was not going to let the opportunity to win the southern hemisphere’s premier club competition slip as he added a Super Rugby title to his URC winner’s medal from the last 12 months. The All Blacks midfield was otherworldly today, producing a nigh-on perfect performance in all facets of the game. He was yet again the ideal foil for Love in the number 12 jersey, taking on a lot of the playmaking duties, carrying strongly and seemingly always making the correct decision. He finished the game with 13 carries, 52 metres, five defenders beaten, four linebreaks, and pitched in with a try and an assist. Barrett was not alone, with Roigard and Love both producing arguably their best performances of the season, in stark contrast to their All Blacks teammate McKenzie on the other side of the pitch. Love claimed the man of the match award for his 25-point haul, which included two tries while he assisted another too. Roigard departed proceedings having controlled the insanely effective Hurricanes’ attack, throwing two try-assist passes but ultimately bossing the tempo from start to finish. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Whilst the Hurricanes backs absolutely deserve the praise that will come their way, All Blacks assistant coaches Jason Ryan and Neil Barnes will be most pleased with what they saw up front. Hooker Asafo Aumua was a one-man wrecking ball once again and won his personal head-to-head with Chiefs star Samisoni Taukei’aho, despite both lineouts faltering at times. Aumua was also part of a ‘Canes pack that had the upper hand at scrum time, though wasn’t properly rewarded for their dominance, while Xavier Numia and Pasilio Tosi were extremely destructive in just about everything they did during their cameos. In the back-row, Flanders was superb in his final outing for the ‘Canes as were his partners in crime Du’Plessis Kirifi and Peter Lakai. The Hurricanes’ attack and backline brilliance stole the spotlight all season and again in the final but so much of their success was rooted in the performances in the forward pack, which certainly deserve their flowers. A team simply cannot score a record-breaking 114 tries in a season if the pack isn’t firing and firing on all cylinders and today, much like it has all season, the Hurricanes pack produced the goods. Furthermore, it wasn’t just the starters as the likes of Tyrel Lomax, Jacob Devery, Siale Lauaki and the first-ever double Hurricanes’ Super Rugby winner Brad Shields picked up from where the starters left off to complete the Chiefs’ embarrassment. title: Louise V. Wiatrak - Medina Gazette
content: Louise V. Wiatrak, 85, of Brunswick, passed away Wednesday, June 17, 2026. She was born in Cleveland on July 17, 1940, to Louis and Margaret (Sadowski) Konopka. Louise is survived by her husband of 64 years, Thomas; daughters, Linda (Steve Kravec) Hennis and Laura (Patrick) Icardi; grandchildren, David (Annie), Steven (Megan), Zach (Keely), Sarah (Matthew), and Jacob (Taylor); great-grandchildren, Claire, Sydney, Jake, Hannah and Elise. Louise was a devoted member of Brunswick United Methodist Church. Her love for her family has always been the driving force in her life. She married her high school sweetheart, Tom, and together they shared a marriage that lasted for 64 years. They enjoyed traveling and making new friends in many different countries. Her unending support for her children and grandchildren was evident in the attendance of nearly every event they participated in. In addition to her family, her love extended to her many cats that she loved throughout her life. Louise started her career as a registered x-ray technician and worked at Southwest General Hospital until she transitioned to working as an MA for Dr. Charles Hoyt. When he retired, his practice was purchased by University Hospitals with the understanding that Louise was part of the deal. She finished her MA career working for Dr. Robert Blankfield. During her years as an MA, she touched many lives and cared for the patients as if they were friends and family because to her, they were. She will be dearly missed. Visitation will be held from 10 to 11 a.m., Friday, June 26, 2026, at Brunswick United Methodist Church, 1395 Pearl Rd., Brunswick, followed by a Memorial Service at 11 a.m. Online condolences and memories may be left for the family at www.WaiteFuneralHome.com

title: Weekend’s hurling fixtures, throw-in times and TV details, including Clare v Dublin - The Irish Times
content: Clare v Dublin, Semple Stadium, Thurles, 7pm (Live on RTÉ 1) Clare and Dublin suffered multiple flesh wounds the last time we saw them. What matters now is how they have healed. In that process Clare hold the aces. It is easier to make excuses for their performance against Cork than for Dublin’s capitulation in the Leinster final. The pivotal game in Clare’s season so far had been eight days earlier against Tipperary and for a team with their age profile their mental and physical resources were simply depleted. Four weeks has allowed time for Mark Rodgers, Ryan Taylor and Darragh Lohan to recover from injuries and for everybody else to catch their breath. It is hackneyed to say that the Clare forward line is among the best in the championship, but the fact is they haven’t clicked since the opening game against Waterford. Shane O’Donnell and Peter Duggan have been below their best, David Reidy has been in and out, David Fitzgerald is a shadow of the player he was two years ago. Diarmuid Stritch and Seán Rynne are young players having a breakthrough season and they were terrific against Tipp; against Cork, though, they couldn’t swim against the tide. They weren’t alone. In Páirc Uí Chaoimh, Clare lost a game they didn’t need to win; it is impossible for Dublin to view the Leinster final in that way. In every respect they were wiped out. They coughed up 4-15 on turnovers, having only conceded 0-11 on turnovers to Kilkenny. Their shots output dropped from 45 to 32 from one game to the next. Against an elite opponent, those numbers are unsustainable. For all the strides that Dublin have made over the last 18 months, they lost the Leinster final in just the same way they have lost other Leinster finals over the last 13 years. For the sake of this group and their future together they can’t afford to implode again. Expect Clare to have straightened themselves out. Verdict: Clare Cork v Offaly, Semple Stadium, Thurles, 3.30pm (Live on RTÉ 1) Offaly’s re-emergence as a competitive force in the Leinster championship has been the most heartening story of the championship. The band of young players that reached three age-grade All-Ireland finals in as many years have more experience at senior level already than their peers in other counties and that is starting to tell. The question is how strong are form lines from the Leinster championship? Kilkenny and Wexford are at their lowest ebb in years and there are queries about Dublin against after the Leinster final. The unvarnished reality is that Cork are the strongest opponents they will have met so far. Cork have made four changes in their front eight, two of them enforced by injury. Brian Roche will not weaken Cork’s centrefield and Alan Walsh deserves his chance in the corner. Offaly took a beating in a challenge match against Clare recently and a similar fate awaits them here.
